steps.input_summary:
Content Strategy input:
- Product Brain
- Trends
- Evergreen Topics
- Anti-repetition Memory

Strategy Items input:
- Content Strategy plan
- Funnel distribution
- Tone / diversity balance

brief.angle: A founder narrates their Tuesday in reverse — every hour they planned to use for growth was swallowed by writing one caption that still isn't done by 6pm. No drama, just a quiet audit of where the day actually went.
brief.topic: The social media task that looks small but quietly consumes your whole Tuesday
brief.pain_point: Creating content takes too many hours every week

brief.angle: A product manager at a two-person SaaS team documents the gap between their content brainstorm on Monday and the reality that nothing was posted by Friday — the ideas existed, the time did not.
brief.topic: Why your content ideas never survive contact with your actual schedule
brief.pain_point: Running out of content ideas

brief.angle: POV: a potential customer discovers a brand through a Google search, clicks their Instagram link, and sees a feed that stopped nine weeks ago. The video walks through exactly what that stranger is thinking — and what decision they make next.
brief.topic: What your business looks like to a stranger who finds your social profile first
brief.pain_point: Social accounts are inactive or inconsistent

brief.angle: An ecommerce brand owner walks through their notes app: 23 saved content ideas, zero turned into posts. The video explores why the backlog keeps growing and why clearing it never makes the priority list.
brief.topic: The content backlog that grows faster than you can clear it
brief.pain_point: Running out of content ideas

brief.angle: A solo founder describes the moment they realized their freelancer relationship required weekly briefs, revision rounds, and approval cycles — more hours spent managing content than they ever spent creating it themselves.
brief.topic: Hiring a freelancer to fix your content — and ending up managing another job
brief.pain_point: Hiring creators or agencies is expensive

brief.angle: A small marketing team lead reflects on the recurring pattern: content production is always the first item bumped when a client call runs long or a product issue needs attention. The slot exists on the calendar; the output never does.
brief.topic: The meeting that replaced your content hour — every single week
brief.pain_point: No time to create content regularly

brief.angle: A practical breakdown — not emotional, just numerical — of the real time and mental load required to produce native content for LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube Shorts simultaneously as a solo operator.
brief.topic: What it actually costs to stay active on four platforms at once without a team
brief.pain_point: Difficulty maintaining a presence across multiple social platforms simultaneously

brief.angle: A straightforward walkthrough of the fenrik Studio intake process: one URL submitted, no brief written, no creative direction given — and what comes back on the other side. Focuses on what the customer does not have to do.
brief.topic: What happens when your content input is just a URL — nothing else
brief.pain_point: Struggling to produce consistent, platform-ready social media content

brief.angle: A bootstrapped app founder ships a major update, sends the changelog to their email list, then realizes they posted nothing on any social channel — the moment passed, and so did the attention window.
brief.topic: The product launch that happened without a single post to support it
brief.pain_point: Social accounts are inactive or inconsistent

brief.angle: A reflective, conversational piece examining the structural reason content keeps getting deprioritized: it has no deadline, no angry customer, and no immediate consequence — until it does.
brief.topic: Why content always gets treated like a side project — even when it's a priority
brief.pain_point: Content production distracts from running the business

brief.angle: An agency owner reflects on a client who paid for social media management for six months and still saw posting gaps — because the agency's bandwidth was spread across too many accounts to maintain genuine frequency for any one of them.
brief.topic: The agency retainer that didn't solve the consistency problem
brief.pain_point: Hiring creators or agencies is expensive

brief.angle: A concrete, no-hype look at what a completed fenrik Studio package contains — video, captions, platform-specific posts — framed as 'here is what you would have spent your week building, delivered instead.'
brief.topic: From website to ready-to-post video: what the output actually looks like
brief.pain_point: Struggling to produce consistent, platform-ready social media content

brief.angle: A content-specific frustration piece: a SaaS marketer explains that the original video took 40 minutes to record and the next three hours were spent resizing, rewriting captions, and figuring out hashtag strategy per platform.
brief.topic: Why reformatting one piece of content for five platforms takes longer than creating it
brief.pain_point: Difficulty maintaining a presence across multiple social platforms simultaneously

brief.angle: A local service business owner recounts a conversation with a long-term customer who admitted they almost switched providers because the business's social feed had gone dark for six weeks — they assumed something was wrong.
brief.topic: The quiet month that made a business look like it stopped caring
brief.pain_point: Social accounts are inactive or inconsistent

brief.angle: A candid look at the in-house content promise: the team agrees it's a priority, someone is nominally responsible, and three months later the account has two posts. The video diagnoses the structural gap — not the motivation gap.
brief.topic: Why 'we'll do content in-house' is the plan that never actually starts
brief.pain_point: Struggling to produce consistent, platform-ready social media content

brief.angle: Reframes the value of a defined deliverable: it's not just about the videos — it's that a fixed package eliminates the open-ended decisions (what to make, how many, for which platforms) that cause teams to stall indefinitely.
brief.topic: Why a fixed video package removes the part of content that actually stalls most teams
brief.pain_point: No time to create content regularly

brief.angle: A founder reflects on the moment they realized they were spending more time thinking about what to post than actually running their business — and that this had been true for months without anyone naming it.
brief.topic: How content production quietly became a second job nobody applied for
brief.pain_point: Content production distracts from running the business

brief.angle: A small marketing team documents a 'content week' they blocked off — the planning, the filming, the editing — and the final output: three posts across two platforms. The math on hours per post is the uncomfortable punchline.
brief.topic: The content sprint that burned out the whole team and produced three posts
brief.pain_point: Creating content takes too many hours every week

brief.angle: A practical, grounded look at the operational shift when a batch of finished content lands in a team's hands — not inspirational, just functional: what gets removed from the weekly to-do list and what that time goes back to.
brief.topic: What 20 ready-to-post videos actually does to a team's weekly workload
brief.pain_point: No time to create content regularly

brief.angle: A solo consultant describes the weekly pattern: energy and ideas on Sunday, a packed client schedule by Monday, and by Wednesday the content slot on the calendar has already been quietly deleted. The cycle repeats.
brief.topic: Why content ideas feel abundant on Sunday and impossible by Wednesday
brief.pain_point: Running out of content ideas

brief.angle: A direct, low-pressure close: the video explains that the barrier most people imagine (the brief, the creative direction, the platform strategy) doesn't exist here. The only input is a URL. The first package costs nothing. The CTA is the whole point.
brief.topic: You already have a website — that's the only thing fenrik Studio needs from you
brief.pain_point: Struggling to produce consistent, platform-ready social media content
